name: The example
why: With capacity 6, the days are [3, 2], [2, 4] and [1, 4]. With 5, it takes four days. If you got 5, your day count is wrong: a parcel that does not fit must start a new day, and then be added to that day.

name: One day
why: With one day, the van must take everything at once, so the answer is the total weight. hi must start at sum(parcels), and hi itself must be a possible answer.

name: A day for every parcel
why: With one day for each parcel, the van only needs to carry the heaviest one. lo must start at max(parcels). If it starts at 0 or 1, the check may accept a van that cannot carry one of the parcels.

name: More days than parcels
why: Extra days do not let the van be smaller than the heaviest parcel. If you got less than 7, your day count does not reject a parcel that is heavier than the capacity.

name: Ten parcels, five days
why: Capacity 15 gives [1 to 5], [6, 7], [8], [9] and [10]. If you got 14 or 16, check the comparison in the loop: a capacity that needs exactly `days` days works.

name: Order matters
why: Parcels must leave in the order they were booked. If you sort them, or pair heavy and light parcels out of order, you get 10. That is not possible with this order.

name: 50,000 parcels, 100 days
why: If you try capacities one by one, starting from max(parcels), you need about 125,000 checks of 50,000 parcels each. That cannot finish in time. Binary search on the capacity needs about 24 checks.

name: One very heavy parcel
show: parcels = 49,999 parcels of 1, then one of 500,000; days = 2
why: The answer is the weight of the heaviest parcel. If this test runs out of time, the search is trying capacities one at a time instead of halving the range.
